stories.title: The Taíno and the Spanish conquest of the Caribbean
stories.where: Baracoa, eastern Cuba (approximate)
facts: The Taíno, an Arawakan-speaking people, lived in what are now Cuba, Jamaica, Hispaniola, Puerto Rico and the Virgin Islands when Columbus arrived; estimates of their number at the time of the Spanish conquest run from about one million to more than three million.
https://www.britannica.com/topic/Taino
Spanish conquistadors began conquering the Taíno in 1493 and forced on them the encomienda system, under which they had to pay tribute and provide labour to the Spanish.
https://www.britannica.com/topic/Taino
Enslavement and starvation under Spanish demands, together with diseases brought from Europe, reduced the Taíno to a few thousand by 1520 and to near extinction by 1550.
https://www.britannica.com/topic/Taino

In 1511 Diego Velázquez set out from Hispaniola to conquer eastern Cuba; Hatuey, a cacique from Hispaniola, had gone ahead to warn its people, fought the Spaniards with guerrilla tactics, and was burned alive at Yara on 2 February 1512.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hatuey

Bartolomé de las Casas went to Hispaniola in 1502, held an encomienda, took part in the conquest of Cuba in 1513, and in 1514 announced that he was giving up his Indian serfs; he wrote his Brevísima relación in 1542.
https://www.britannica.com/biography/Bartolome-de-Las-Casas

The crown's attempts to curb the encomienda's abuses, the Laws of Burgos (1512–13) and the New Laws of 1542, failed in the face of colonial opposition; Britannica says the system in practice became a form of enslavement.
https://www.britannica.com/topic/encomienda
The Taíno also fought back: La Navidad, the settlement Columbus left on Hispaniola in 1492, was destroyed by Indigenous people by the following year, after its men had seized women and gold.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Navidad
The cacique Enriquillo led a rebellion against the Spanish colonists on Hispaniola from 1519 to 1533.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enriquillo

voices.text: Then thus, he said, they adore a certain Covetous Deity, whose cravings are not to be satisfied by a few moderate offerings, but they may answer his Adoration and Worship, demand many unreasonable things of us, and use their utmost endeavors to subjugate and afterwards murder us. Then taking up a Cask or Cabinet near at hand, full of Gold and Gems, he proceeded in this manner: This is the Spaniards God, and in honour of him if you think well of it, let us celebrate our Arcytos (which are certain kinds of Dances and caprings used among them); and by this means his Deity being appeas'd, he will impose his Commands on the Spaniards that they shall not for the future molest us
voices.who: Hatuey, as recorded by Bartolomé de las Casas (speaking to his people in Cuba before the Spaniards landed; the 1689 translation spells his name Hathney)
voices.date: c. 1511; written 1542, published 1552; this English translation 1689
voices.doc: A Brief Account of the Destruction of the Indies, 'Of the Isle of Cuba' (London: R. Hewson, 1689), Project Gutenberg eBook #20321

voices.text: After that Hathney had been silently pensive sometime, he askt the Monk whether the Spaniards also were admitted into Heaven, and he answering that the Gates of Heaven were open to all that were Good and Godly, the Cacic replied without further consideration, that he would rather go to Hell then Heaven, for fear he should cohabit in the same Mansion with so Sanguinary and Bloody a Nation.
voices.who: Hatuey, bound to the stake, as recorded (in reported speech) by Bartolomé de las Casas; Las Casas arrived in Cuba after the execution and was not present
voices.doc: A Brief Account of the Destruction of the Indies, 'Of the Isle of Cuba' (1689), Project Gutenberg eBook #20321

witness.text: I once saw Four or Five of their most Powerful Lords laid on these Gridirons, and thereon roasted, and not far off, Two or Three more over-spread with the same Commodity, Man's Flesh; but the shril Clamours which were heard there being offensive to the Captain, by hindring his Repose, he commanded them to be strangled with a Halter. The Executioner (whose Name and Parents at Sevil are not unknown to me) prohibited the doing of it; but stopt Gags into their Mouths to prevent the hearing of the noise (he himself making the Fire) till that they dyed, when they had been roasted as long as he thought convenient.
witness.who: Bartolomé de las Casas, on Hispaniola; a colonist and encomendero there before he turned against the conquest

witness.text: Once it so hapned, that the Citizens of a Famous City, distant Ten Miles from the place where we then resided, came to meet us with a splendid Retinue, to render their Visit more Honourable, bringing with them delicious Viands, and such kind of Dainties, with as great a quantity of Fish as they could possibly procure, and distributing them among us; but behold on a sudden, some wicked Devil possessing the minds of the Spaniards, agitated them with great fury, that I being present, and without the least Pretence or Occasion offered, they cut off in cold Blood above Three Thousand Men, Women and Children promiscuously, such Inhumanities and Barbarisms were committed in my sight, as no Age can parallel.
witness.who: Bartolomé de las Casas, who was with the Spanish force in Cuba

witness.text: A certain Person here in the same Isle constituted to exercise a kind of Royal Power, hapned to have Three Hundred Indians fall to his share, of which in Three Months, through excessive labour, One Hundred and Sixty were destroy'd, insomuch that in a short space there remained but a tenth part alive, namely Thirty, but when the number was doubled, they all perisht at the same rate, and all that were bestow'd upon him lost their lives, till at length he paid his last Debt to Nature and the Devil.
witness.who: Bartolomé de las Casas, on forced labour in Cuba

official.text: If you do so, you will do well, and that which you are obliged to do to their Highnesses, and we in their name shall receive you in all love and charity, and shall leave you your wives, and your children, and your lands, free without servitude, that you may do with them and with yourselves freely that which you like and think best, and they shall not compel you to turn Christians, unless you yourselves, when informed of the truth, should wish to be converted to our Holy Catholic Faith, as almost all the inhabitants of the rest of the islands have done.
official.who: The Requerimiento (Requirement), written by the crown jurist Juan López de Palacios Rubios and read to Indigenous peoples to demand their submission; translated by Arthur Helps, The Spanish Conquest in America, vol. 1 (1855), p. 381; it was drafted after most of the island conquests and was first read on the mainland in 1514

official.text: we shall take you and your wives and your children, and shall make slaves of them, and as such shall sell and dispose of them as their Highnesses may command; and we shall take away your goods, and shall do you all the mischief and damage that we can, as to vassals who do not obey, and refuse to receive their lord, and resist and contradict him; and we protest that the deaths and losses which shall accrue from this are your fault, and not that of their Highnesses, or ours, nor of these cavaliers who come with us.
official.who: The Requerimiento, on what would follow if the people refused or delayed; Helps's translation (1855), p. 382

stories.warn: The Las Casas passages are from a 1689 English version, made by way of other European translations rather than straight from the Spanish and printed under the anti-Catholic title Popery Truly Display'd; spelling is the original's (it gives Hatuey as 'Hathney'). Hatuey's words were written down by Las Casas some thirty years later and are not a transcript.
disputed: How many Taíno there were. Las Casas wrote that three million people lived on Hispaniola alone, and Britannica gives estimates of one million to more than three million Taíno in all; a 2021 ancient-DNA study in Nature argues that estimates of hundreds of thousands or millions for islands such as Hispaniola are too large, while stating that the devastating impact of colonisation and systematic killing is indisputable.

Disease or violence and forced labour. Some historians hold that epidemic disease (smallpox, influenza, measles, typhus) was the overwhelming cause of the collapse; others, such as Andrés Reséndez, argue that disease alone does not explain it, that smallpox is not recorded in the islands until about 1519, and that slavery and forced labour were a major killer. Las Casas's Brief Account, written to move the king, attributes the deaths almost entirely to Spanish cruelty.

Did Las Casas exaggerate? Critics note that he contrasted Spanish cruelty with Indigenous goodness in an exaggerated way to persuade, and that Protestant printers and engravers such as Theodor de Bry used his book to build the anti-Spanish 'Black Legend'; on the other side, he presented himself as an eyewitness of much of what he describes, and modern historians who reject his figures still accept the scale of the destruction.
stories.blind: The Taíno left no writing, so their words survive only as Spanish writers chose to record them, Hatuey's through a friar who campaigned against the conquest and wrote decades later. The women forced into labour, the people shipped away as slaves and the Africans brought in to replace the dead are almost silent in this record.
reading: Las Casas, A Brief Account of the Destruction of the Indies, 1689 translation (Project Gutenberg)
Helps, The Spanish Conquest in America, vol. 1 (1855, scan), with the full Requerimiento
Fernandes et al., A genetic history of the pre-contact Caribbean (Nature, 2021, open access)

stories.title: The Zong massacre
stories.where: Accra, Gold Coast (Ghana), where the Zong set sail; the killings took place at sea beyond Jamaica
facts: The Zong was a Dutch slave ship captured by the British off the African coast in 1781 with 244 enslaved Africans in its hold, then sold to a syndicate of Liverpool merchants who renamed and insured it.
https://www.britannica.com/event/Zong-massacre
It traded for 198 more enslaved men, women and children along the coast and left Accra on the Gold Coast on 18 August 1781, bound for Black River, Jamaica.
https://www.britannica.com/event/Zong-massacre

After a navigational error carried the ship past Jamaica, the captain, Luke Collingwood, proposed and the crew agreed on 29 November to throw enslaved people overboard: 54 women and children that night, 42 men on 1 December, and a third group after that, while 10 others jumped into the sea.
https://www.britannica.com/event/Zong-massacre

The owners claimed insurance for 132 people; a jury at Guildhall, London, found for them on 6 March 1783, but at the King's Bench hearing in May Lord Mansfield ordered a new trial after it emerged that rain had fallen before the last group was killed, and no record survives of a new trial being held.
https://www.britannica.com/event/Zong-massacre
On 19 March 1783 Olaudah Equiano told the anti-slave-trade campaigner Granville Sharp about the killings; Sharp tried without success to have the crew prosecuted for murder.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zong_massacre
In 1791 Parliament prohibited insurers from reimbursing ship owners for enslaved Africans killed by being thrown overboard.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zong_massacre

voices.text: The closeness of the place, and the heat of the climate, added to the number in the ship, which was so crowded that each had scarcely room to turn himself, almost suffocated us. This produced copious perspirations, so that the air soon became unfit for respiration, from a variety of loathsome smells, and brought on a sickness among the slaves, of which many died, thus falling victims to the improvident avarice, as I may call it, of their purchasers. This wretched situation was again aggravated by the galling of the chains, now become insupportable; and the filth of the necessary tubs, into which the children often fell, and were almost suffocated. The shrieks of the women, and the groans of the dying, rendered the whole a scene of horror almost inconceivable.
voices.who: Olaudah Equiano (Gustavus Vassa), describing his own crossing as a boy, a generation before the Zong; he was not on that ship
voices.doc: The Interesting Narrative of the Life of Olaudah Equiano, ch. 2 (Project Gutenberg eBook #15399)

voices.text: One day, when we had a smooth sea and moderate wind, two of my wearied countrymen who were chained together (I was near them at the time), preferring death to such a life of misery, somehow made through the nettings and jumped into the sea: immediately another quite dejected fellow, who, on account of his illness, was suffered to be out of irons, also followed their example; and I believe many more would very soon have done the same if they had not been prevented by the ship's crew, who were instantly alarmed.
voices.who: Olaudah Equiano, on the same crossing
voices.doc: The Interesting Narrative of the Life of Olaudah Equiano, ch. 2 (Project Gutenberg eBook #15399)

witness.text: March 19.—Gustavus Vasa, a Negro, called on me, with an account of one hundred and thirty Negroes being thrown alive into the sea, from on board an English slave ship.
witness.who: Granville Sharp, campaigner against slavery, in his own notes, printed by Prince Hoare, Memoirs of Granville Sharp (1820), p. 236

witness.text: which master, mate, and crew, on pretence of necessity (lest there should be a want of water), wilfully and deliberately destroyed one hundred and twenty-two Negro slaves, by casting them alive (as it is deposed) into the sea, with their hands bound or fettered, to deprive them of all possibility of escaping. Having been earnestly solicited and called upon by a poor Negro for my assistance, to avenge the blood of his murdered countrymen, I thought it my duty to spare neither labour nor expense in collecting all the information concerning this horrible transaction that I could possibly procure, for the sake of national justice
witness.who: Granville Sharp, letter to the Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty asking for a murder prosecution, as printed by Hoare (1820), p. 242; the figure 122 is as printed there (Sharp's covering letter on p. 241 says 132)

official.text: left to the jury, was, whether it was from necessity; for they had no doubt (though it shocks one very much) that the case of slaves was the same as if horses had been thrown overboard. It is a very shocking case.
official.who: Lord Mansfield, Lord Chief Justice, summing up the first trial at the King's Bench hearing on the insurers' appeal (Gregson v Gilbert), from notes taken in court for Granville Sharp, printed by Hoare (1820), p. 241

official.text: The question after all is, was it voluntary, or an act of necessity? This is a case of chattels or goods. It is really so: it is the case of throwing over goods; for to this purpose, and the purpose of the insurance, they are goods and property: whether right or wrong, we have nothing to do with it. This property—the human creatures, if you will—have been thrown overboard: whether or not for the preservation of the rest, that is the real question.
official.who: John Lee, Solicitor-General, arguing for the ship's owners at the same hearing, as printed by Hoare (1820), p. 239

stories.warn: The words spoken at the 1783 hearing come from notes taken in court for Granville Sharp, who wanted the crew tried for murder, as printed in 1820; they are not an official law report. Period sources use the word 'Negro'.
disputed: How many were killed. The owners claimed for 132, the figure the National Maritime Museum uses; Britannica counts 143 from the groups recorded, the first mate James Kelsall later gave 'the outside number' as 142, and Sharp's letter to the Admiralty as printed in 1820 says 122. The surviving accounts come largely from Kelsall and the passenger Robert Stubbs, who both had reason to clear themselves.

Was there a water shortage? The owners argued that throwing people overboard was a necessity to save the rest; the insurers showed that rain had fallen before the last killings, the ship reached Jamaica with water to spare, and Britannica calls the crew's calculations highly suspect.

Where Equiano was born. He wrote that he was born about 1745 in Essaka, in the Igbo country; the scholar Vincent Carretta found a baptism register ('born in Carolina') and a 1773 ship's muster that he argued point to a birth in America, while other scholars, such as Paul Lovejoy, hold that the weight of evidence supports an African birth.
stories.blind: Not one word survives from the people thrown into the sea, or from the 208 who reached Jamaica and were sold; the ship's log went missing, and what happened on board is known from the crew who did it, the lawyers who argued over the money and the campaigner who tried to have them tried. Equiano speaks for the captives of the Middle Passage, but he was not on the Zong.
reading: Hoare, Memoirs of Granville Sharp (1820, scan), ch. 8 'The Ship Zong'
Documents relating to the case of the ship Zong, REC/19 (National Maritime Museum, Greenwich)

stories.title: The overthrow of the Hawaiian Kingdom
stories.where: ʻIolani Palace, Honolulu, Hawaiʻi
facts: Liliʻuokalani came to the throne in January 1891, the first woman to hold it, and tried to restore some of the power the monarchy had lost under her brother Kalākaua.
https://www.britannica.com/biography/Liliuokalani

When she moved to bring in a new constitution, a Committee of Safety of non-native businessmen and politicians, with Sanford Dole as head of the government it set up, and supported by the US Minister John Stevens and marines landed from the warship USS Boston, overthrew her on 17 January 1893 and proclaimed a Provisional Government.
https://www.archives.gov/education/lessons/hawaii-petition
President Cleveland rejected the annexation treaty and sought to restore the Queen, but Dole refused, saying Cleveland had no authority to interfere.
https://www.britannica.com/biography/Liliuokalani

In 1895 an armed rising in the Queen's name, led by the royalist Robert Wilcox, was put down; the Queen was held under arrest and on 24 January 1895 signed an abdication to win pardons for her jailed supporters.
https://www.britannica.com/biography/Liliuokalani

In 1897 the Hui Aloha ʻĀina petition against annexation was signed by 21,269 native Hawaiians, more than half of the 39,000 native and part-Hawaiians counted that year, and the annexation treaty failed in the Senate.
https://www.archives.gov/education/lessons/hawaii-petition
Hawaii was annexed instead by a joint resolution of Congress, the Newlands Resolution, which needed only a simple majority and was signed by President McKinley on 7 July 1898.
https://www.archives.gov/education/lessons/hawaii-petition

voices.text: I, Liliuokalani, by the grace of God and under the constitution of the Hawaiian kingdom Queen, do hereby solemnly protest against any and all acts done against myself and the constitutional government of the Hawaiian kingdom by certain persons claiming to have established a Provisional Government of and for this kingdom. That I yield to the superior force of the United States of America, whose Minister Plenipotentiary, His Excellency John L. Stevens, has caused United States troops to be landed at Honolulu, and declared that he would support the said Provisional Government.
voices.who: Queen Liliʻuokalani, protest signed at six in the evening on the day of the overthrow
voices.doc: As printed in Hawaii's Story by Hawaii's Queen (1898), Appendix B, 'Extracts from statement made by the Queen to Minister Blount'

voices.text: To other usurpations of authority on the part of those whose love for the institutions of their native land we could understand and forgive we had submitted. We had allowed them virtually to give us a constitution, and control the offices of state. Not without protest, indeed; for the usurpation was unrighteous, and cost us much humiliation and distress. But we did not resist it by force. It had not entered into our hearts to believe that these friends and allies from the United States, even with all their foreign affinities, would ever go so far as to absolutely overthrow our form of government, seize our nation by the throat, and pass it over to an alien power.
voices.who: Queen Liliʻuokalani
voices.doc: Hawaii's Story by Hawaii's Queen, chapter LVII, 'Hawaiian Autonomy'

voices.text: I declare such a treaty to be an act of wrong toward the native and part-native people of Hawaii, an invasion of the rights of the ruling chiefs, in violation of international rights both toward my people and toward friendly nations with whom they have made treaties, the perpetuation of the fraud whereby the constitutional government was overthrown and, finally, an act of gross injustice to me.
voices.who: Queen Liliʻuokalani, protest against the annexation treaty, delivered to the State Department
voices.doc: Hawaii's Story by Hawaii's Queen, chapter LV, 'My Official Protest to the Treaty'

witness.text: From a careful inquiry I am satisfied that it would be defeated by a vote of at least two to one. If the votes of persons claiming allegiance to foreign countries were excluded, it would be defeated by more than five to one. The undoubted sentiment of the people is for the Queen, against the Provisional Government and against annexation. A majority of the whites, especially Americans, are for annexation.
witness.who: US official critical of the overthrow: James H. Blount, special commissioner sent by President Cleveland, report to Secretary of State Gresham (on annexation, if put to a vote)

witness.text: By an act of war, committed with the participation of a diplomatic representative of the United States and without authority of Congress, the Government of a feeble but friendly and confiding people has been overthrown. A substantial wrong has thus been done which a due regard for our national character as well as the rights of the injured people requires we should endeavor to repair. The provisional government has not assumed a republican or other constitutional form, but has remained a mere executive council or oligarchy, set up without the assent of the people.
witness.who: US official critical of the overthrow: President Grover Cleveland, message to Congress

official.text: Not content with her victory Her Majesty proceeded on the last day of the session to arbitrarily arrogate to herself the right to promulgate a new constitution, which proposed, among other things, to disfranchise over one-fourth of the voters and the owners of nine-tenths of the private property of the Kingdom, to abolish the elected upper house of the legislature and to substitute in place thereof an appointive one, to be appointed by the Sovereign.
official.who: Proclamation of the Committee of Safety establishing the Provisional Government, which went on to declare 'The Hawaiian monarchical system of Government is hereby abrogated'

official.text: The main part of the opponents of annexation are the lower class of natives, led by unscrupulous foreigners, of little property, mostly from California, Australia, and Canada, who wish to maintain the Hawaiian monarchy and its corruptions for their own unworthy purposes, and who think their opportunities for power and spoliation will be gone if annexation becomes a fact. The Hawaiian pear is now fully ripe, and this is the golden hour for the United States to pluck it.
official.who: John L. Stevens, US Minister in Honolulu, dispatch to Secretary of State Foster

today.text: apologizes to Native Hawaiians on behalf of the people of the United States for the overthrow of the Kingdom of Hawaii on January 17, 1893 with the participation of agents and citizens of the United States, and the deprivation of the rights of Native Hawaiians to self-determination
today.who: US Congress, Apology Resolution, Public Law 103-150 (which adds that nothing in it is intended to settle any claims against the United States)

stories.warn: Hawaiian names appear as the 1890s English-language documents spelled them, without the ʻokina and kahakō (Liliuokalani for Liliʻuokalani).
disputed: What the US minister and the troops did. Blount's 1893 report found that Minister Stevens acted without authority and landed the marines on a false or exaggerated pretext to back the conspirators, and that this was decisive; the Senate's Morgan Report of 1894 contradicted it and cleared everyone involved except the Queen. A later federal Native Hawaiians Study Commission report concluded that the truth lies somewhere between the two.

Whether annexation was lawful. Annexation came by a joint resolution of Congress after a treaty failed to win two-thirds of the Senate, and without any vote of the Hawaiian people; the Hawaiian sovereignty movement still disputes its legality, while US courts (DeLima v. Bidwell, 1901; Arakaki v. Lingle, 2007) have treated it as valid.

Restoration and amnesty. When Cleveland's minister Albert Willis offered to restore her if she granted amnesty to everyone responsible, the Queen first replied that Hawaiian law called for property confiscation and death for treason, which lost her the administration's goodwill; she then changed her position on amnesty, but the Provisional Government refused to reinstate her.
stories.blind: The record that survives in English is mostly the Queen's own and that of American officials on both sides. The 21,269 people who signed the 1897 petitions, and the Hawaiian-language newspapers of the time, speak mainly in Hawaiian, and most of their words have not been published in English.
reading: Liliʻuokalani, Hawaii's Story by Hawaii's Queen (1898), full text (A Celebration of Women Writers, University of Pennsylvania)
Foreign Relations of the United States, 1894, Appendix II: Affairs in Hawaii, including the Blount Report (Office of the Historian)
The 1897 Petition Against the Annexation of Hawaii (US National Archives)

stories.title: The Tulsa race massacre
stories.where: Greenwood District, Tulsa, Oklahoma, United States
facts: By early 1921 most of Tulsa's ten thousand African American residents lived in the Greenwood District, home to two newspapers, several churches, a library branch and scores of Black-owned businesses.
https://www.okhistory.org/publications/enc/entry?entry=TU013

On 31 May 1921, after the Tulsa Tribune reported that Dick Rowland, a Black shoe shiner, had attempted to rape a white elevator operator, hundreds of whites gathered at the county courthouse demanding that he be handed over; armed Black men, many of them First World War veterans, went there to help protect him, and a shot fired as they left began the fighting.
https://www.okhistory.org/publications/enc/entry?entry=TU013

At daybreak on 1 June thousands of armed whites, some of them deputised by the police that night, poured into Greenwood, looting homes and businesses and setting them on fire; Black Tulsans fought to defend their district but were outgunned and outnumbered.
https://www.okhistory.org/publications/enc/entry?entry=TU013

In eighteen hours more than one thousand homes and businesses were destroyed; thousands of Tulsans were held under armed guard and the city was placed under martial law, and thousands spent the following winter living in tents.
https://www.okhistory.org/publications/enc/entry?entry=TU013

A state grand jury indicted about 70 men, many of them Black leaders of Greenwood; Police Chief John Gustafson was charged with dereliction of duty and corruption, convicted and removed, but no white person was ever sent to prison for the killing, burning and looting.
https://www.justice.gov/crt/media/1383756/dl
Rowland was exonerated; the white establishment tried to force the Black community to relocate, but Greenwood residents began rebuilding within days.
https://www.okhistory.org/publications/enc/entry?entry=TU013

voices.text: After watching the men unload on First Street where we could see them from our windows, we heard such a buzzing noise that on running to the door to get a better view of what was going on, the sights our eyes beheld made our poor hearts stand still for a moment. There was a great shadow in the sky and upon a second look we discerned that this cloud was caused by fast approaching aeroplanes. It then dawned upon us that the enemy had organized in the night and was invading our district the same as the Germans invaded France and Belgium. The firing of guns was renewed in quick succession. People were seen to flee from their burning homes, some with babes in their arms and leading crying and excited children by the hand; others, old and feeble, all fleeing to safety.
voices.who: Mary E. Jones Parrish, who taught typing in Greenwood and fled with her young daughter
voices.doc: Events of the Tulsa Disaster, 'My Experience in Tulsa', pp. 9–10 (transcribed from the scan; OCR errors corrected)

voices.text: From a 10-room and basement modern brick home, I am now living in what was my coal barn. From a 5-chair white enamel barber shop, 4 baths, electric clippers, electric fan, 2 lavatories and shampoo stands, 4 workmen, double marble shine stand, a porter and an income of over $500 or $600 per month, to a razor, strop and folding chair on the sidewalk. I feel that corrupt politics is the cause of the whole affair, for if the authorities had taken the proper steps in time the whole matter could have been prevented.
voices.who: C. L. Netherland, proprietor of a barber shop on Greenwood, statement collected by Mary E. Jones Parrish
voices.doc: Events of the Tulsa Disaster, p. 42 (transcribed from the scan; OCR errors corrected)

witness.text: It is highly doubtful if the exact number of casualties will ever be known. The figures originally given in the press estimate the number at 100. The number buried by local undertakers and given out by city officials is ten white and twenty-one colored. For obvious reasons these officials wish to keep the number published as low as possible, but the figures obtained in Tulsa are far higher. Fifty whites and between 150 and 200 Negroes is much nearer the actual number of deaths.
witness.who: Walter F. White, assistant secretary of the NAACP, who went to Tulsa to investigate, 'The Eruption of Tulsa', The Nation, p. 910

official.text: While we find the presence of the armed negroes was the direct cause of the riot, we further find that there existed indirect causes more vital to the public interest than the direct cause. Among these were agitation among the negroes of social equality, and the laxity of law enforcement
official.who: Report of the Tulsa County grand jury, printed in the Tulsa World under the headline 'Grand Jury Blames Negroes for Inciting Race Rioting; Whites Clearly Exonerated' (as quoted by the Library of Congress)

today.text: On the night of May 31, 1921, a violent attack by as many as 10,000 white Tulsans destroyed the thriving Black community of Greenwood, Oklahoma—a prosperous area often referred to as “Black Wall Street.” The attack, which lasted into the afternoon of June 1, was so systematic and coordinated that it transcended mere mob violence. White men murdered hundreds of Black residents, burned businesses and homes to the ground, and left survivors without resources or recourse. In the aftermath, authorities failed to offer meaningful help, and efforts to seek justice through the courts foundered.
today.who: US Department of Justice, Civil Rights Division, report under the Emmett Till Unsolved Civil Rights Crime Act, executive summary (it also found that no prosecution is now possible)

stories.warn: The 1921 texts use the words of their time, including 'Negro' and 'colored'; the grand jury and the press then called the massacre a 'riot'.
disputed: How many died. In 1921 city officials gave out 10 white and 21 Black dead; Walter White, investigating that June, put it at about 50 whites and 150 to 200 Black people; the Oklahoma Historical Society says credible estimates range from 50 to 300, and the Justice Department (2025) says as many as 300, perhaps more, and that an accurate toll may never be agreed because bodies were dumped in the river and buried in unmarked mass graves.

The graves. Long-held beliefs that victims were buried in unmarked graves were supported by evidence a team of scientists and historians found after the state commission was set up in 1997; the City of Tulsa's excavations at Oaklawn Cemetery have found previously unknown graves and identified massacre victims by DNA, and the search continues.

The aeroplanes. Survivors such as Mary Jones Parrish saw planes over Greenwood, and Walter White wrote that some said they were used for bombing; the Oklahoma Historical Society says only that some participants have claimed planes were used in the attack, and the Justice Department could not settle whether planes dropped incendiaries or how often they fired shots, though it notes that several eyewitnesses said they saw incendiary materials dropped.

The 'To Lynch Negro Tonight' editorial. Eyewitnesses said the Tulsa Tribune printed it on 31 May; the Library of Congress notes that no copy has been found, since parts of that day's surviving paper were torn out, while the front-page story accusing Rowland is confirmed.
stories.blind: Survivors' own words from 1921 survive mainly because Mary Jones Parrish collected them in a small, self-published book; Tulsa's two Black newspapers were burned and could not report, the official record (grand jury, police, white press) blamed the victims, and for decades the subject was kept quiet in Tulsa, so many of the dead are still unnamed.
reading: Mary E. Jones Parrish, Events of the Tulsa Disaster (1922), scan (Internet Archive)
Tulsa Race Massacre (Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture, Oklahoma Historical Society)
US Department of Justice, Review and Evaluation: Tulsa Race Massacre (2025)
Tulsa Race Massacre: Newspaper Complicity and Coverage (Library of Congress)

stories.title: The fall of Jerusalem to the First Crusade
stories.where: Old City of Jerusalem (approximate)
facts: In 1095, at the Council of Clermont, Pope Urban II urged Christians to undertake an armed pilgrimage to Jerusalem, which had been under Muslim rule since the 7th century.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Crusade
The Fatimids of Egypt had taken Jerusalem in August 1098; on 7 June 1099 the Crusader army, reduced to perhaps 1,200–1,500 cavalry and 12,000 foot soldiers, encamped before it.
https://www.britannica.com/event/Crusades/The-siege-of-Jerusalem

On 15 July Godfrey's men took a sector of the walls; the Muslim governor surrendered to Raymond in the Tower of David and was escorted out with his bodyguard, but Tancred's promise of protection in the Aqsa Mosque was disobeyed, and Muslim and Jewish men, women and children died in the general slaughter that followed.
https://www.britannica.com/event/Crusades/The-siege-of-Jerusalem

According to the Damascus chronicler Ibn al-Qalanisi, Jews who had taken refuge in their synagogue died when the Crusaders burned it; some Muslims and Jews survived by escaping or being taken prisoner for ransom, and a letter of the Karaite elders of Ascalon tells of efforts to ransom Jewish captives and send them to Alexandria.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Crusade
The governor had expelled the city's Eastern Christians before the siege, so they escaped the massacre.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Crusade
Godfrey was elected to govern with the title Defender of the Holy Sepulchre, and most Crusaders, having fulfilled their pilgrimage vows, went home.
https://www.britannica.com/event/Crusades/The-siege-of-Jerusalem

voices.text: Les personnes qui avaient quitté la Syrie, arrivèrent à Bagdad, au mois de ramadan (fin de juillet ou commencement d'août). Elles se présentèrent au divan (conseil d'administration), et y firent un récit qui arracha des larmes de tous les yeux. La douleur était dans tous les cœurs. Ces personnes, le vendredi qui suivit leur arrivée, restèrent dans la grande mosquée, invoquant la miséricorde divine. Elles pleuraient, et le peuple entier pleurait avec elles; elles racontèrent les malheurs qui avaient frappé les Musulmans de nobles et vastes contrées, le massacre des hommes, l'enlèvement des femmes et des enfants, et le pillage des propriétés.
voices.who: Refugees from Syria in Baghdad, as recorded by Ibn al-Athir. In plain English: 'The people who had fled Syria reached Baghdad in Ramadan and came before the council, where their story brought tears to every eye. On the Friday after they arrived they stayed in the great mosque calling on God's mercy, weeping, and the whole people wept with them; they told of the calamities that had struck the Muslims of noble and wide lands: the men massacred, the women and children carried off, the property plundered.'
voices.doc: Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-tarikh, tr. Reinaud, Recueil des historiens des croisades, Historiens orientaux, vol. 1 (1872), p. 199

voices.text: Vos frères, dans la Syrie, n'ont pour se reposer que le dos de leurs chameaux ou les entrailles des vautours. Les Romains les couvrent d'opprobre ; et vous, vous laissez traîner votre robe dans la mollesse, comme quelqu'un qui n'aurait rien à craindre ! Que de sang a été répandu! que de femmes à qui on n'a laissé, pour protéger leur pudeur, que la paume de leurs mains !
voices.who: The poet al-Muzaffar al-Abiwardi, a contemporary, in verses on the fall of Jerusalem quoted by Ibn al-Athir ('Romains' renders the Arabic Rum, here the Christian invaders); al-Abiwardi wrote in Iraq and was not himself a refugee. In plain English: 'Your brothers in Syria have nowhere to rest but the backs of their camels or the bellies of vultures. The Rum heap shame on them, while you trail your robes in idle ease as if you had nothing to fear. How much blood has been shed! How many women have been left nothing but the palms of their hands to cover their modesty!'
voices.doc: Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-tarikh, tr. Reinaud, Recueil des historiens des croisades, Historiens orientaux, vol. 1 (1872), p. 200

witness.text: La ville sainte fut prise du côté du nord, dans la matinée du vendredi 22 du mois de schaban (15 juillet). Aussitôt la foule prit la fuite. Les Francs restèrent une semaine dans la ville, occupés à massacrer les Musulmans. Une troupe de Musulmans s'était retirée dans le Mihrab de David, et s'y était fortifiée. Elle se défendit pendant trois jours. Les Francs ayant offert de les recevoir à capitulation, ils se rendirent et eurent la vie sauve; on leur permit de sortir pendant la nuit, et ils se retirèrent à Ascalon.
witness.who: Ibn al-Athir (1160–1233), historian of Mosul, writing about 120 years later. In plain English: 'The holy city was taken from the north on the morning of Friday 22 Sha'ban (15 July). At once the crowd fled. The Franks stayed a week in the city, busy massacring the Muslims. A band of Muslims had shut themselves in the Mihrab of David and held out for three days. When the Franks offered them terms they surrendered and were spared; they were let out by night and went to Ascalon.'

witness.text: Les Francs massacrèrent plus de soixante et dix mille Musulmans dans la mosquée Alacsa: parmi eux on remarquait un grand nombre d'imams, d'oulamas (savants), et de personnes d'une vie pieuse et mortifiée, qui avaient quitté leur patrie pour venir prier dans ce noble lieu.
witness.who: Ibn al-Athir. In plain English: 'The Franks massacred more than seventy thousand Muslims in the Aqsa mosque; among them were many imams, scholars, and people of pious and ascetic life who had left their homelands to pray in that noble place.'

witness.text: Godefroy ayant pris en main le glaive de Vespasien, se précipita de toute sa force contre les infidèles. Il en immola 65,000 dans le temple, sans compter ceux qui périrent dans les autres parties de la ville. C'est ainsi que fut prise Jérusalem, et le tombeau du Christ, notre Dieu, délivré de la servitude des musulmans. C'est pour la troisième fois que l'épée de Vespasien sévissait contre Jérusalem depuis que le Seigneur avait été crucifié.
witness.who: Matthew of Edessa, Armenian Christian chronicler of the early 12th century, writing in Edessa, later under Frankish rule, and not uncritical of the Franks (tr. Édouard Dulaurier, 1858). In plain English: 'Godfrey, taking up the sword of Vespasian, threw himself with all his strength on the infidels. He slaughtered 65,000 of them in the temple, not counting those who died in the rest of the city. So Jerusalem was taken, and the tomb of Christ our God delivered from the bondage of the Muslims. It was the third time since the Lord was crucified that the sword of Vespasian had raged against Jerusalem.'

official.text: On the roof of the Temple a great number of pagans of both sexes had assembled, and these were taken under the protection of Tancred and Gaston of Beert. Afterward, the army scattered throughout the city and took possession of the gold and silver, the horses and mules, and the houses filled with goods of all kinds. Later, all of our people went to the Sepulchre of our Lord, rejoicing and weeping for joy, and they rendered up the offering that they owed. In the morning, some of our men cautiously ascended to the roof of the Temple and attacked the Saracens, both men and women, beheading them with naked swords; the remainder sought death by jumping down into the temple.
official.who: The Gesta Francorum, written by an anonymous knight in the Crusader army (tr. August C. Krey, 1921)

official.text: But these were small matters compared to what happened at the Temple of Solomon, a place where religious services are ordinarily chanted. What happened there? If I tell the truth, it will exceed your powers of belief. So let it suffice to say this much, at least, that in the Temple and porch of Solomon, men rode in blood up to their knees and bridle reins. Indeed, it was a just and splendid judgment of God that this place should be filled with the blood of the unbelievers, since it had suffered so long from their blasphemies.
official.who: Raymond of Aguilers, chaplain to Count Raymond of Toulouse, an eyewitness in the Crusader army (tr. August C. Krey, 1921)

official.text: A new day, new joy, new and perpetual gladness, the consummation of our labor and devotion, drew forth from all new words and new songs. This day, I say, will be famous in all future ages, for it turned our labors and sorrows into joy and exultation; this day, I say, marks the justification of all Christianity, the humiliation of paganism, and the renewal of our faith.
official.who: Raymond of Aguilers on the pilgrims' devotion at the Holy Sepulchre after the capture (tr. August C. Krey, 1921)

official.text: Accordingly, the Lord, pleased at this humility, granted the city with His enemies to us on the eighth day after our humiliation, on this day, to wit, when the primitive Church was expelled from Jerusalem, the day when the festival of the Dispersion of the Apostles is celebrated by many of the faithful. And, if you desire to know what was done about the enemy whom we found there, know that in the portico of Solomon and in his Temple, our men rode in the blood of the Saracens up to the knees of the horses.
official.who: Letter of Archbishop Daimbert of Pisa, Duke Godfrey, Count Raymond of St Gilles and 'all the army of God' to the Pope (Paschal II), printed by Krey as the 'Official summary of the Crusade'
official.date: 1099, after the battle of Ascalon (12 August), from Laodicea

stories.note: Research in progress: the Jewish testimony of 1099, Cairo Geniza letters such as that of the Karaite elders of Ascalon, is available only in modern copyrighted translations, so none is quoted here.
stories.warn: Ibn al-Athir wrote in Mosul over a century after the events; his account and al-Abiwardi's verses are quoted in J.-T. Reinaud's French translation, and Matthew of Edessa in Édouard Dulaurier's French, each with a plain-English gloss. The Crusader texts are August C. Krey's 1921 English. The sources of the time call Muslims 'Saracens', 'pagans' or 'infidels'.
disputed: The death toll. Ibn al-Athir counts more than 70,000 killed in the Aqsa mosque and Matthew of Edessa 65,000 in the temple. Modern historians call such figures unrealistic for a city of perhaps 30,000 and estimate 3,000 to 10,000 dead; Britannica writes of hundreds of men, women and children killed.

Was the massacre exceptional? Benjamin Kedar, working mainly from the Latin sources, concluded it was considerably more extensive than in other towns. Konrad Hirschler argues that the early Arabic sources show a massacre no greater than at Antioch, Caesarea or Ma'arrat al-Nu'man, and that it came to be remembered as a full-scale massacre only decades later.

Blood 'up to the knees'. The Crusaders' own texts disagree on the depth: the Gesta Francorum says ankles, Raymond of Aguilers knees and bridle reins, the leaders' letter the horses' knees. The historian Thomas Madden calls these descriptions fantastical and impossible, while stressing that the massacre and its bloodshed were real.

The synagogue. The Damascus chronicler Ibn al-Qalanisi says the Jews gathered in their synagogue and the Franks burned it over their heads; a Jewish letter written about two weeks later confirms the burning but does not mention people inside.
stories.blind: Almost none of the people killed or driven out left their own account. The Muslim histories were written decades or a century later, far away in Damascus, Baghdad or Mosul; the Jewish letters from the Cairo Geniza survive only in modern translations; and the most detailed accounts of the slaughter are by clergy and knights of the victorious army, who celebrated it.
reading: August C. Krey, The First Crusade: The Accounts of Eye-Witnesses and Participants (1921), full text
Recueil des historiens des croisades, Historiens orientaux, vol. 1 (1872)

stories.title: The Peasants' Revolt
stories.where: Smithfield, London, England (approximate)
facts: The rising's immediate cause was the unpopular poll tax of 1380, which brought to a head discontent that had grown since the Black Death, including anger at the Statute of Labourers (1351), which tried to fix maximum wages during the labour shortage.
https://www.britannica.com/event/Peasants-Revolt

That third poll tax was a flat 12 pence on every person over 15; many in the south-east evaded it by refusing to register, and when the royal official John Bampton tried to collect unpaid tax at Brentwood, Essex, on 30 May 1381, the confrontation turned violent and spread across the south-east.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peasants%27_Revolt

On 13 June the Kentish rebels under Wat Tyler entered London, massacred some Flemish merchants and razed John of Gaunt's Savoy Palace; on 14 June, while Richard II met the Essex men at Mile End and promised the abolition of serfdom, rebels in the Tower beheaded the chancellor, Archbishop Simon Sudbury, and the treasurer, Sir Robert Hales.
https://www.britannica.com/event/Peasants-Revolt
The hunt for Flemings went on into 14 June: in one city ward the bodies of 40 Flemings were piled in the street, and 35 were killed at the church of St Martin Vintry.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peasants%27_Revolt

At Smithfield on 15 June Tyler was cut down in the king's presence by the mayor, William Walworth, and later beheaded; the priest John Ball was tried at St Albans and hanged, drawn and quartered on 15 July.
https://www.britannica.com/event/Peasants-Revolt
On 2 July the charters granted under duress were formally revoked, and by November at least 1,500 people had been executed or killed in battle.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peasants%27_Revolt

voices.text: Ah, ye good people, the matters goeth not well to pass in England, nor shall not do till everything be common, and that there be no villains nor gentlemen, but that we may be all united together, and that the lords be no greater masters than we be. What have we deserved, or why should we be kept thus in servage? We be all come from one father and one mother, Adam and Eve: whereby can they say or shew that they be greater lords than we be, saving by that they cause us to win and labour for that they dispend?
voices.who: John Ball, as recorded by Jean Froissart (Froissart says Ball preached this to villagers coming out of church on Sundays in Kent)
voices.doc: The Chronicles of Froissart, tr. Lord Berners, ed. G. C. Macaulay, 'How the Commons of England Rebelled against the Noblemen' (Harvard Classics vol. 35, 1910)
voices.lic: Public domain (Berners translation 1523–25; Macaulay edition 1895; Project Gutenberg ebook 13674)

voices.text: They are clothed in velvet and camlet furred with grise, and we be vestured with poor cloth: they have their wines, spices and good bread, and we have the drawing out of the chaff and drink water; they dwell in fair houses, and we have the pain and travail, rain and wind in the fields; and by that that cometh of our labours they keep and maintain their estates: we be called their bondmen, and without we do readily them service, we be beaten; and we have no sovereign to whom we may complain, nor that will hear us nor do us right.
voices.who: John Ball, as recorded by Jean Froissart
voices.doc: The Chronicles of Froissart, tr. Lord Berners, ed. G. C. Macaulay (Harvard Classics vol. 35, 1910)
voices.lic: Public domain (Berners translation 1523–25; Project Gutenberg ebook 13674)

voices.text: We will that ye make us free for ever, ourselves, our heirs and our lands, and that we be called no more bond nor so reputed.
voices.who: The rebels at Mile End answering Richard II's question 'what lack ye?', as recorded by Jean Froissart
voices.doc: The Chronicles of Froissart, tr. Lord Berners, ed. G. C. Macaulay, 'How the Nobles of England were in Great Peril' (Harvard Classics vol. 35, 1910)

voices.text: John Schepe, some time St. Mary's priest of York, and now of Colchester, greeteth well John Nameless, and John the Miller, and John the Carter, and biddeth them that they beware of guile in borough, and stand together in God's name, and biddeth Piers Plowman go to his work, and chastise well Hobbe the Robber [i.e. Robert Hales the treasurer], and take with you John Trueman and all his fellows, and no mo, and look that ye shape you to one head and no mo.

These gluttons took him and strake off his head, and also they beheaded the lord of Saint John's and a friar minor, master in medicine, pertaining to the duke of Lancaster

Withdraw you home into your own houses and into such villages as ye came from, and leave behind you of every village two or three, and I shall cause writings to be made and seal them with my seal, the which they shall have with them, containing everything that ye demand; and to the intent that ye shall be the better assured, I shall cause my banners to be delivered into every bailiwick, shire and countries.

official.text: miseri, et odibiles terrae marique, nec vivere quidem digni, petitis dominis comparari. [...] Rustici quidem fuistis et estis; in bondagio permanebitis, non ut hactenus, sed incomparabiliter viliori. Nam ad hoc dum vivimus, et regno, Deo dante, praefuerimus, sensu, viribus, et catallis nostris, elaborabimus vos suppeditare
official.who: Richard II to envoys of the Essex rebels at Waltham who asked him to confirm the Mile End promises, as reported in Latin by Thomas Walsingham, monk of St Albans. In plain English: 'Wretches, hateful on land and sea, not even worthy to live, you ask to be made equal to your lords. [...] Peasants you were and peasants you are; you will remain in bondage, not as before but incomparably viler. For as long as we live and by God's grace rule this realm, we will labour with mind, strength and wealth to hold you down.'

official.text: Prelates, lords temporal, citizens, knights and burgesses responded with one voice that the repealing of the Charters had been wisely done. And they added that such a manumission of serfs could not have been made without the consent of those who had the main interest in the matter. And, for their own parts, they would never consent of their own free will, nor otherwise, nor ever would do it, even if they all had to live and die in one day.
official.who: Parliament's answer when the king's ministers asked whether the serfs might be freed, from the Rolls of Parliament as rendered by Charles Oman (1906)

stories.warn: Froissart's English is Lord Berners' Tudor translation; John Ball's sermon and the words at Mile End are Froissart's reconstruction from informants, not transcripts, and Froissart calls the rebels 'gluttons' and 'unhappy people'. Ball's letter is in Charles Oman's modernised English. Richard II's reply survives only in the Latin of Thomas Walsingham, a chronicler hostile to the rebels, with a plain-language gloss.
disputed: How many rose. The chroniclers give round numbers: Froissart has 60,000 marching on London and more than threescore thousand on Blackheath, while Walsingham puts 200,000 at Blackheath. Court records studied by modern historians show a broader rising than the chroniclers' picture of rural serfs, including artisans and village officials, but no reliable total.

Did the revolt achieve anything? Britannica says it failed completely as a social revolution and the king's promises were promptly forgotten, but that it stopped the poll tax, which did not return until 1641. It was once seen as the cause of serfdom's end; modern historians are less certain and say serfdom declined after 1381 mainly for economic reasons, vanishing in the 15th century, though peasants invoked the memory of the revolt when bargaining over rents.

Who killed the Flemings. Froissart blames the rebel bands; the historian Rodney Hilton argues the London attacks may have been coordinated by the city's weavers' guilds, commercial rivals of the Flemish weavers.
stories.blind: No account sympathetic to the rebels survives: their words come to us through chroniclers who despised them, through indictments, and through John Ball's letters, kept because they were used against him. Women who took part, such as Johanna Ferrour, appear only in court records, and the Flemish victims are counted, not named.
reading: Charles Oman, The Great Revolt of 1381 (1906), full text
Froissart, Wat Tyler's Rebellion, tr. Lord Berners (Project Gutenberg)

stories.title: King Afonso of Kongo protests the Portuguese slave trade
stories.where: Mbanza Kongo, Zaire Province, Angola (capital of the Kongo kingdom)
facts: Afonso I (Mvemba a Nzinga, c. 1460–1542) was baptised with his father by Portuguese priests in 1491 and became king of Kongo sometime between 1506 and 1509, after defeating his half brother Mpanzu a Kitima at the capital, Mbanza Kongo.
https://www.britannica.com/biography/Afonso-I-king-of-Kongo-kingdom
Under the Regimento of 1512 agreed with Manuel I of Portugal, Kongo accepted Portuguese institutions, granted Portuguese subjects extraterritorial rights and supplied slaves to Portuguese traders.
https://www.britannica.com/biography/Afonso-I-king-of-Kongo-kingdom

Afonso took part in the trade himself: after a campaign against the Kingdom of Ndongo in 1512 he told King Manuel he had sent him 410 slaves captured in the war, and he sent slaves to Portugal to pay for the education of Kongolese notables and to buy goods.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_I_of_Kongo

In 1526, on discovering that Portuguese merchants were buying and exporting people who had been enslaved illegally, Afonso set up an administrative system to oversee the slave trade, which reached considerable proportions during his reign.
https://www.britannica.com/biography/Afonso-I-king-of-Kongo-kingdom

A US Library of Congress country study says the Portuguese crown came to view Kongo primarily as a source of slaves, and that Afonso's complaints about the trade's effects in his lands were largely ignored.
https://countrystudies.us/angola/5.htm
The remains of Mbanza Kongo, in northern Angola, were inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2017 as the 'Vestiges of the Capital of the former Kingdom of Kongo'.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%27banza-Kongo

voices.text: E nam avemos este dano por tamanho como he que os ditos mercadores leuam cada dia nossos naturaes filhos da terra e filhos de nossos fidallgos e vassallos e nossos parentes por que hos ladrões e homens de maa concyencya os furtam com desejo daver asy as cousas e mercadoryas desse Reyno que sam desejossos, os furtam e lhos trazem a vender em tanta maneira Senhor he esta coruçam e devasydade que nosa terra se despouoa toda o que vossa alteza nam deue aver por bem nem seu seruiço.
voices.who: Afonso I (Mvemba a Nzinga), king of Kongo, to King João III of Portugal, written down by his secretary João Teixeira (in short: this harm is not as great as the fact that the merchants carry off our people every day, sons of the land, sons of our nobles and vassals, even our own kin; thieves steal them to get Portuguese goods, and the corruption is so great that our land is being emptied of people)
voices.doc: Letter of 6 July 1526, printed in Paiva Manso, História do Congo (Documentos), Lisbon 1877, doc. XXVII, p. 54 (transcribed from the scan)

voices.text: E por Isto Evytarmos nam temos necesydade desses Reynos mães que de padres e algumas poucas pessoas pêra emsynarem nas escollas nem menos de nenhumas mercadoryas somente vynho e farynha pêra o santo sacramento, porque pedymos a vossa alteza nos queira ajudar e fauorecer neste casso Em mandar a seus feytores que nam mande ca mercadores nem mercadorias, porque nossa vontade he que nestes Reynos nam aja trato de esprauos nem sayda pêra elles.
voices.who: Afonso I, same letter (in short: to prevent this we need nothing from your kingdoms but priests and a few people to teach in the schools, and no goods except wine and flour for the Mass; we ask you to order your agents to send no merchants or goods here, because it is our will that in these kingdoms there be no trade in slaves nor any outlet for them)

voices.text: muitos nossos naturaes pollo dessejo muito que tem das mercadorias e coussas desses Reynos que os vossos a estees tragem e a esta coussa e por satysfazerem seu desordenado apetite furtam muitos dos nossos naturaees forros e isemtos e muytas vezes se comteçe furtarem fidallgos e filhos de fidallgos e parentes nossos e os leuam a vender aos homens brancos que em nossos Reynos Estam E lhos trazem esscõdidos e outros de noyte por nam serem conhecidos. E tamto que sam em poder dos ditos homens brancos ssam logo fferados e marcados com fogo
voices.who: Afonso I to João III (in short: many of our people, craving the goods your subjects bring, steal free subjects of ours, often even nobles, sons of nobles and our own kin, and sell them to the white men in our kingdoms, bringing them hidden or by night so they are not recognised; and as soon as they are in the white men's hands they are branded with fire)
voices.doc: Letter of 18 October 1526, Paiva Manso, História do Congo (Documentos), 1877, doc. XXIX, p. 57 (transcribed from the scan)

voices.text: E por evitarmos tam grande mall possemos por ley que todo homem bramco que Em nossos rreynos Esteuer e conprara peças per qualquer maneyra que seja que primeiro ho faça ssaber a três fidallgos e oficiaes de nossa corte em quem Este casso comfyamos, a saber a dom pedro manipanza E a dom manoell manissaba nosso merinho mor E a gonçalo pires nosso armador mor pêra verem as ditas peças se ssam catiuos se forras
voices.who: Afonso I, same letter, describing the law he made (in short: to avoid so great an evil we decreed that any white man in our kingdoms who buys 'pieces' (enslaved people) must first report it to three nobles and officers of our court, Dom Pedro Manipanza, Dom Manuel Manissaba, our chief bailiff, and Gonçalo Pires, our chief outfitter, to see whether they are captives or free). The letter goes on to say that people cleared this way could be shipped
voices.doc: Paiva Manso, História do Congo (Documentos), 1877, doc. XXIX, p. 57 (transcribed from the scan)

official.text: Itaque volente Deo tota Guineae régio feliciter peragrata est, in qua Rex de Manicongo cum ingentibus populis ipsi subditis, qui se ad eius autoritatem ac obdientiam contulerat, sacro baptismate suscepto, Christianus effectus est
official.who: King João III of Portugal, letter in Latin to Pope Clement VII on Portugal's discoveries, as printed in Paiva Manso, História do Congo (Documentos), 1877, doc. XXXIII, p. 62 (in short: so, God willing, the whole region of Guinea has been happily explored, in which the King of Kongo, with the great peoples subject to him who had placed themselves under his authority and obedience, received holy baptism and became a Christian). In this passage, six years after Afonso's protests, the crown's account to Rome presents Kongo as a missionary success; the slave trade is not mentioned

stories.warn: Afonso's letters are quoted in early 16th-century Portuguese with the irregular spelling of the manuscripts, and João III's letter in Latin, all as printed by Paiva Manso in 1877; the plain-English summaries in 'who' are the site's own, not translations. Afonso's letters were written down by his secretary João Teixeira. 'Peças' (pieces) was the traders' word for enslaved people.
disputed: How far Afonso opposed slavery. On 6 July 1526 he asked that there be no slave trade in Kongo at all; by 18 October he described a law under which white men could buy and ship people once three court officials had checked they were lawful captives, not free Kongolese. Britannica says he set up a system to oversee the trade, and the historian Linda Heywood argues that Kongo's kings at first protected freeborn Kongolese while selling foreign-born captives; Afonso himself had sent Manuel I 410 war captives in 1512. A US Library of Congress study instead stresses that his complaints against the trade were largely ignored by the Portuguese crown.

How many people were taken. Afonso wrote in 1526 that his land was being depopulated. The historian Linda Heywood judges that most of the slaves sold at the time came from outside Kongo. None of these sources gives a reliable count of people shipped from Kongo in the 1520s.
stories.blind: What survives is the king's side, dictated to Portuguese-trained secretaries and kept in the royal archives in Lisbon, and the Portuguese crown's replies; the people seized, both free Kongolese and the foreign captives sold through Kongo, left no words of their own. Afonso speaks as a king who himself sold war captives.
reading: Linda Heywood, 'Slavery and its transformation in the Kingdom of Kongo: 1491–1800', Journal of African History (2009)
stories.note: Research in progress: the Portuguese crown's own words on the Kongo slave trade (Manuel I's Regimento of 1512 to Simão da Silva and João III's reply to Afonso of late 1529) are not in Paiva Manso's 1877 edition and are still being sought in a public-domain printing.

stories.title: The Ludlow massacre
stories.where: Ludlow Tent Colony Site, Las Animas County, Colorado, United States
facts: About 10,000 coal miners led by the United Mine Workers of America struck in southern Colorado from September 1913 over low pay and working conditions; evicted from the company towns, they and their families lived in tent colonies, the largest of them at Ludlow with about 1,200 people.
https://www.britannica.com/event/Ludlow-Massacre

The Colorado Fuel and Iron Company, which employed about 7,000 workers, rejected the union's demands, which included enforcement of the eight-hour workday and the right to choose their own housing and doctors.
https://home.nps.gov/articles/000/war-in-the-coalfields-the-ludlow-massacre-and-its-impact-on-the-eight-hour-workday.htm

Governor Elias Ammons sent the Colorado National Guard to keep the peace, but the mine owners had already arranged with the state to pay for the deployment, and the Colorado Encyclopedia says the troops caused more trouble.
https://coloradoencyclopedia.org/article/ludlow-massacre

On 20 April 1914 a day-long battle broke out between the Guard and the colony; three strike leaders, including Louis Tikas, were captured and killed, and that evening the tents were soaked in kerosene and burned, and 11 children and 2 women were found suffocated and burned in a cellar under one tent.
https://www.britannica.com/event/Ludlow-Massacre

In retaliation, armed miners attacked antiunion officials, strikebreakers and mines and held an area about 50 miles long; Britannica says as many as 50 people died before President Woodrow Wilson sent federal troops to restore order.
https://www.britannica.com/event/Ludlow-Massacre

Of the 408 strikers arrested, 332 were indicted for murder; of those present at Ludlow only the strike leader John Lawson was convicted, and the Colorado Supreme Court overturned the conviction. Twenty-two National Guardsmen, including 10 officers, were court-martialed.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow_Massacre

voices.text: Well, in the evening when the fire started I came out of my tent; it was all on fire, and I came out of my tent, and as I was coming out of my tent under that tank there was a lot of militiamen, and I was running out and hollering with my three children, and they hollered at me to get out of the way and they were shooting at me and I ran into this place.

There were 11 children and 2 women suffocated with the smoke where I was. I lost two children in this cave when the tent burned. I don't know where my husband was at this time. I looked up out of the hole and saw the soldier set fire to the tent with a match. I lost everything I had in this fire.

voices.doc: Industrial Relations: Final Report and Testimony, vol. 8 (1916), p. 7099

voices.text: I had six children in the well with me. My husband was killed there; he was coming to see me and take care of me and the children, and he was shot in the back. He was crying all day for me and the children.

voices.doc: George P. West, Report on the Colorado Strike (US Commission on Industrial Relations, 1915), p. 130

witness.text: Accounts vary as to who fired the first shot on the morning of the tragedy, but it is established that the first offensive movement was the occupation of a hill near the tent colony by militiamen in full view of the strikers, the planting of a machine gun there, and the exploding of two dynamite bombs by the militia. These bombs had been made by Linderfelt to be used as signals to call the militia and mine guards from near-by mines and camps, but the strikers did not know their purpose.
witness.who: George P. West, investigator for the US Commission on Industrial Relations, Report on the Colorado Strike, p. 127 (West's report is sharply critical of the companies and the Guard)

witness.text: Inflamed by what they considered the wanton slaughter of their women, children and comrades, the miners attacked mine after mine, driving off or killing the guards and setting fire to the buildings. At the Empire mine of the Southwestern Fuel Company near Aguilar the President of the company, J. W. Siple, with twenty men and eight women and children, took refuge in the mine stope after the shaft house and buildings had been burned and dynamited.
witness.who: George P. West, Report on the Colorado Strike, p. 133, on the strikers' armed revolt in the days after Ludlow

official.text: When the detail left, the Greeks, over the protest of their leader, ran for their guns and threatened to fight. Major Hamrock brought the detachment from Cedar Hill down to Water Tank Hill, in plain view of the colony, preparatory to searching the colony for its alleged prisoner. Some excitable women, seeing these troops on the hill, and nervous over the actions of the Greeks, rushed into the colony, screaming that the soldiers were about to attack. Thereupon the Greeks filed out of the colony to a railroad cut, and soon afterwards fired the first shots of the battle against the soldiers.
official.who: Special Board of Officers of the Colorado National Guard (Maj. Edward J. Boughton, Capt. William C. Danks, Capt. Philip S. Van Cise), appointed to investigate the battle, findings, p. 24

official.text: The origin of the fire in the tent colony was accidental; that is to say, it was due either to an overturned stove, an explosion of some sort, or the concentrated fire directed at one time against some of the tents. The fire began in the corner nearest the Cross-Roads. Afterwards it was deliberately spread by the combatants. During the fire the soldiers, upon learning that women and children were still in the colony, went through the tents, calling upon all the persons in the colony to come forth, and with difficulty rescuing men, women and children to the number of some twenty-five or thirty, including one William Snyder and his family. Then the tents were fired.
official.who: Special Board of Officers of the Colorado National Guard, findings, pp. 24–25

official.text: Feeling that this board of officers was not constituted to determine possible guilt or innocence, we recommend that a general court martial be appointed to try all officers and enlisted men participating in the treatment and killing of prisoners, and the burning and looting of the tent colony.
official.who: Special Board of Officers of the Colorado National Guard, recommendation A, p. 27

today.text: On the morning of April 20, National Guardsmen aligned with the Colorado Fuel & Iron Company attacked the Ludlow Tent Colony to try and break the UMWA strike, killing 21 people (including 11 children) in what became known as the “Ludlow Massacre.” This act of collective violence ignited 10 days of continuous warfare in Colorado, until President Woodrow Wilson ordered Federal troops to disarm both sides and restore order.
today.who: US National Park Service, American Battlefield Protection Program, on a 2024 preservation planning grant for the Ludlow Tent Colony Site

stories.warn: The 1914–15 texts keep the witnesses' own speech ('I seen'). The Guard officers' report speaks of 'the Greeks' as a group and elsewhere calls the strikers 'ferocious foreigners'; it is quoted as the official account of its time, not endorsed.
disputed: Who fired first on 20 April. The Guard's board of officers found that Greek strikers in a railroad cut fired the first shots; the Commission's investigator George P. West wrote that accounts varied but that the first offensive moves (a machine gun on a hill, two dynamite bombs) were the militia's; Britannica says the Guard opened fire after a dispute over a man the miners would not hand over, while the Colorado Encyclopedia says nobody knows who fired the first shot.

How many died. West counted five strikers, one boy and thirteen women and children, with one militiaman killed; the Colorado Encyclopedia says at least nineteen, including one guardsman; the National Park Service says 21, including 11 children; Britannica says 25, 3 of them Guard troops. For the ten days of fighting that followed, Britannica gives as many as 50 dead, and the Colorado Encyclopedia says the number cannot be determined but was certainly more than at Ludlow itself.

How the tents caught fire. The board of officers called the fire accidental, then deliberately spread, and said soldiers rescued some 25 or 30 people; West cited testimony that militiamen fired the tents on their officers' orders, and Alcarita Pedregon swore she saw a militiaman set her tent alight with a match; the Colorado Encyclopedia says Guardsmen burned the tents thinking the colony had been abandoned.
stories.blind: The survivors who speak here are women, several of whom toured and testified with the union's support (one told the Commission the union paid her expenses); the Greek, Italian and Mexican miners who did the fighting, and the mine guards and strikebreakers killed in the ten days afterwards, left almost no first-hand words.
reading: George P. West, Report on the Colorado Strike (1915, scan)
Ludlow: report of the Special Board of Officers (1914, scan)
Commission on Industrial Relations testimony, vol. 9 (Petrucci and others, scan)

stories.title: The "comfort women": Japan's system of military sexual slavery
stories.where: Seoul, South Korea, where survivors first spoke out (approximate); comfort stations ran wherever Japan's forces were based, from China and Korea to Burma, Indonesia and the Pacific islands
facts: "Comfort women" is a euphemism for the women who provided sexual services to Japanese Imperial Army troops and generally lived under conditions of sexual slavery; the great majority were from Korea, then ruled by Japan, with others from China, Taiwan and elsewhere in Asia, including Japanese women and Dutch women in Indonesia.
https://www.britannica.com/topic/comfort-women

The UN Special Rapporteur dates the first comfort stations to Shanghai in 1932, says the plan was revived after Japanese troops captured Nanking in 1937, and lists stations in China, Taiwan, Borneo, the Philippines, many Pacific islands, Singapore, Malaya, Burma and Indonesia.
https://digitallibrary.un.org/record/228137/files/E_CN.4_1996_53_Add.1-EN.pdf?version=1

The same 1996 report identifies three ways women were obtained: women already working as prostitutes, women lured with offers of well-paid work as cooks, cleaners or restaurant staff, and large-scale coercion and abduction in countries under Japanese control.
https://digitallibrary.un.org/record/228137/files/E_CN.4_1996_53_Add.1-EN.pdf?version=1

Britannica says the women typically lived in harsh conditions, raped continually and beaten or murdered if they resisted; according to several reports, notably the 1996 UN study, many were executed at the end of the war, and many survivors abroad were simply abandoned.
https://www.britannica.com/topic/comfort-women
On 14 August 1991 Kim Hak-sun disclosed in a public broadcast that she had been a 'comfort woman'; she joined a lawsuit against the Japanese government that year and died on 16 December 1997.
https://www.kyeol.kr/en/boards/bd_en_look_hist/462

Japan's foreign ministry says the Asian Women's Fund, set up in 1995 by Japan's people and government, paid 'atonement money' to 285 women, and that under the December 2015 Japan–South Korea agreement Japan gave 1 billion yen to a South Korean foundation, which Seoul announced in 2018 it would dissolve.
https://www.mofa.go.jp/policy/postwar/page22e_000883.html

voices.who: A South Korean survivor, as quoted in the UN report

witness.text: Early in May of 1942 Japanese agents arrived in Korea for the purpose of enlisting Korean girls for "comfort service" in newly conquered Japanese territories in Southeast Asia. The nature of this "service" was not specified but it was assumed to be work connected with visiting the wounded in hospitals, rolling bandages, and generally making the soldiers happy. The inducement used by these agents was plenty of money, an opportunity to pay off the family debts, easy work, and the prospect of a new life in a new land - Singapore. On the basis of these false representations many girls enlisted for overseas duty and were rewarded with an advance of a few hundred yen.
witness.who: US Office of War Information, Psychological Warfare Team, Japanese Prisoner of War Interrogation Report No. 49, p. 1, written by T/3 Alex Yorichi after questioning 20 Korean women captured near Myitkyina, Burma (scan of the US National Archives copy, via UCLA's Comfort Women Resource Center)

witness.text: The "house master" received fifty to sixty per cent of the girls' gross earnings depending on how much of a debt each girl had incurred when she signed her contract. This meant that in an average month a girl would gross about fifteen hundred yen. She turned over seven hundred and fifty to the "master". Many "masters" made life very difficult for the girls by charging them high prices for food and other articles.
witness.who: The same US report, p. 3; UCLA's annotation notes that the women were probably questioned through the couple who ran their brothel, and the author also called the women's life in Burma 'near-luxury' compared with other places

official.text: The then Japanese military was, directly or indirectly, involved in the establishment and management of the comfort stations and the transfer of comfort women. The recruitment of the comfort women was conducted mainly by private recruiters who acted in response to the request of the military. The Government study has revealed that in many cases they were recruited against their own will, through coaxing, coercion, etc., and that, at times, administrative/military personnel directly took part in the recruitments.
official.who: Chief Cabinet Secretary Yohei Kono, statement on the result of the Japanese government's study (the Kono Statement), Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Japan

official.text: The issue of comfort women, with an involvement of the Japanese military authorities at that time, was a grave affront to the honor and dignity of large numbers of women, and the Government of Japan is painfully aware of responsibilities from this perspective. today.text: Despite such sincere efforts by the Government of Japan, there are claims that can hardly be said to be based on historical facts, such as the allegations of “forceful taking away” of comfort women and “sex slaves” as well as the figures “200,000 persons” or “several hundred thousands” for the total number of comfort women.
